libraries.group: The standard library, always in scope

modules.brief: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace.
modules.detail:
Reading is the cheap direction of this sandbox and writing is the expensive one, so a program that reads a dozen files to decide what to change is well shaped, while one that rewrites forty large files in a single turn will exhaust its fuel budget.

Nothing here places anything in the agent's context window. `views::open_file` is the call that does.

modules.brief: Run shell commands in the workspace.
modules.detail:
One function, and the way a program reaches everything gg has no tool for: a build, a test run, `git`, `curl`, a package manager. The workspace is the working directory.

A non-zero exit is a *result* rather than a failure, because deciding whether a build or a test run passed is the single most common thing a program does with one.

modules.brief: The epic and issue board, on which work is decomposed into dispatchable units.
modules.detail:
An issue is heavyweight and self-contained: its scope, non-scope and completion criteria are exactly what a delegated child agent is briefed from, which is why `create_issue` asks for more than `tasks::add_task` does.

Two of `IssuePatch`'s fields are three-way, and Rust has an `enum` for exactly that: `TextEdit` leaves, empties or replaces a description, and `EpicAssignment` leaves, detaches or regroups an epic. Neither needs a sentinel.

modules.brief: A private task list, kept as a directed acyclic graph rather than as a list of lines.
modules.detail:
Every task may name the tasks that must finish before it, and an edge that would close a cycle is refused.

One spelling here is worth reading twice. `TaskPatch`'s description is a three-way edit, and `TextEdit` says all three without a sentinel: `Keep` keeps the description that is there, `Clear` empties it, `Set` replaces it.

modules.brief: Durable memories, which survive a context compaction.
modules.detail:
A run picks one of three memory strategies and binds only that strategy's functions, so `memories::list()` is the honest answer to what memory can do here. The scratchpad keeps every memory in the context window (`write_memory`, `update_memory`); the two file-shaped strategies keep the contents outside it (`create_memory`, `read_memory`, `edit_memory`), one behind an index that is always in context and one behind `search_memories`. `delete_memory` is bound under all three.

Every mutation hands back the budget after it, so a program can decide whether to write another memory by reading numbers rather than by parsing a sentence about them.

modules.brief: Show a file, a computed value, or a function's documentation.
modules.detail:
A view is the only way material enters the agent's context window.

Under responses as code a whole program's output would otherwise collapse into one anonymous blob of logs, charged to one band, attributable to nothing and closable by nothing. A view restores what tool calling gave for free: one message per view, carrying the band it is charged to and the selector it can be closed by.

A program's own output is unreadable by the model that wrote it, and a view is the only way a value it computed reaches that model. On this arm the point is hard to miss: `println!` reaches nobody at all, because `wasm32-unknown-unknown` has no standard output to write to.

modules.brief: Manage the agent's own context window.
modules.detail: These are the only calls whose effect is on the conversation rather than on the workspace. They are worth making from a program precisely because a program can decide *when* to: read a set of files, extract what matters, then evict the views, all in one turn.

modules.brief: Delegate work to child agents, and hand this session's own turn to another agent.
modules.detail:
`wait_for_subagents` can dominate a turn's wall clock — it blocks while real agents run — and the run's budget keeps ticking while it does. A program should therefore spawn broadly and wait once, rather than spawn-and-wait in a loop.

The brief is where this arm's types earn their keep: a child is briefed either with a self-contained `Brief::Prompt` or with a board `Brief::Issue`, and because that choice is an `enum` rather than two optional arguments, "both" and "neither" are programs that do not compile.

modules.brief: Read the skills this run authored.
modules.detail: The names available are listed in the system prompt, and an unknown one comes back as `NotFound` carrying the full list.

modules.brief: Fetch a program that already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run.
End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role.
modules.detail:
Under responses as code every reply is a program, so there is no prose turn that could mean "the work is done" — a model that answers "task complete" has written a reply that failed to be a program, not an ending. These are the calls that mean it, and a run binds only the group its agent's role has: an agent doing work gets `finish`, and a reviewer gets `approve` and `request_changes` instead.

None of them stops the program. Whatever follows an ending still runs, so an ending belongs last — and a program that then fails has its ending revoked along with everything else it decided.

modules.brief: The types every other module's signatures name: how a call fails, and what a directory lists.
modules.detail:
A capability module owns the types it produces, so `files::FileRead` belongs to `files` and `board::IssueCreated` to `board`. These three belong to none of them because they belong to all of them: every function in this SDK returns `Result<_, ToolError>`, and every module's `list` returns `FunctionSummary`.

They are the one part of the surface a program writes unqualified. `gg::prelude` re-exports them by name, because a `match` on an error code that had to spell out a module would be a `match` nobody writes.

meta.name: list
meta.doc:
List the functions this module offers, each with a one-line summary.

Only the functions this run actually bound are returned, so the directory never names a call the program cannot make. One function's full signature, argument descriptions and types are opened as a view with `views::open_docs_view`.

functions.name: read_file
functions.brief: Read a file, as either a `FileRead::Text` or a `FileRead::Image`.
functions.detail:
Which of the two comes back is detected from the file's bytes, never from the extension, so a mislabelled picture is still a picture. The enum is closed, so an ordinary `match` needs no catch-all:

```
match files::read_file("logo.png", files::ReadOptions::default())? {
    files::FileRead::Text(text) => views::open_text("logo", &text.contents)?,
    files::FileRead::Image(picture) => views::open_text("logo", &picture.label)?,
}
```

A relative path resolves against the workspace; an absolute one is read as given, so anything else in this container — an offloaded command's output under `/tmp/gg-shell`, say — is readable. This call hands bytes to the program and places nothing in the context window; reading a picture describes it and shows nothing, so a file only read here is a file nobody has looked at.

# Errors

`NotFound` for a missing path.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to read; `files::ReadOptions::default()` reads the whole file.

functions.name: read_text_file
functions.brief: Read a text file and hand back its contents directly.
functions.detail:
`read_file` without the narrowing, for the common case: the same read, the same window, the same cost.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when the path names a picture, which `read_file` inspects instead and `views::open_file` displays.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to read; `files::ReadOptions::default()` reads the whole file.

functions.name: write_file
functions.brief: Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing what is there.
functions.detail: Writing is the expensive direction of this sandbox: rewriting more than a few dozen large files in one program exhausts its fuel budget, so a large rewrite is best split across several turns.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write, relative to the workspace or absolute. Parent directories are created.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

functions.name: edit_file
functions.brief: Replace the one exact occurrence of some text in a file with something else.
functions.detail:
Widening the surrounding context until the match is unique is the way to disambiguate; counting occurrences is not.

# Errors

`NotFound` when the text does not appear, and `Conflict` — with the number of matches — when it appears more than once.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to edit.

parameters.name: old_string
parameters.doc: The exact text to find, whitespace included. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: new_string
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place. An empty string deletes the match.

functions.name: list_dir
functions.brief: List a directory, sorted by name; `None` lists the workspace root.
functions.detail: Each entry carries a bare `name` — join it with the directory that was listed — and its `kind`. An empty directory is an empty `Vec`, not a failure.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The directory to list, relative to the workspace or absolute; `None` lists the workspace root.

functions.name: run
functions.brief: Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace and hand back its merged stdout and stderr.
functions.detail:
A non-zero exit is not a failure: read `exit_code` on the result. Only a process that could not be launched, or one the timeout killed, is an `Err`.

This run may **offload** shell output — the `shell` tool's own description says which mode is in force. Under `offload`, `output` holds only the tail that fits and ends with a note naming the two files the command's full stdout and stderr were written to. Under `adaptive`, the default, a command that succeeded returns no output at all, only that note, and one that failed returns the tail. Grepping the named files is cheaper than re-running the command.

# Errors

`LimitExceeded` when the timeout killed the process, and `IoError` when it could not be launched.

parameters.name: command
parameters.doc: The command line, run by `sh -c` with the workspace as its working directory.

parameters.name: timeout_secs
parameters.doc: How long to let it run, in seconds, before killing it. `None` takes gg's default of 120, clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

functions.name: create_epic
functions.brief: Create an epic to group related issues, and hand back the id its prefix resolved to.
functions.detail:
`prefix` is 3-6 letters naming the epic; it is upper-cased and becomes the epic's id, which is also what its issues are numbered from — a prefix of `auth` gives issues `AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, and so on.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when the prefix is not 3-6 letters or a required field is blank, `Conflict` when another epic already holds the prefix, and `LimitExceeded` at the board's epic cap.

parameters.name: prefix
parameters.doc: 3-6 letters naming it. Upper-cased, it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the body of work.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: What the epic covers, for a reader who has not seen its issues.

functions.name: create_issue
functions.brief: Create a self-contained, dispatchable issue, and hand back the id the board assigned it.
functions.detail:
The id is numbered under its epic's prefix (`AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, …), or under `ISSUE` when it has no epic. It is the board's to choose, so it is worth keeping: blocking a later issue on this one, and waiting for it, both take it. `in_scope`, `out_of_scope` and `completion_criteria` are what a child agent is briefed from, so they are written for a reader with no other context.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when a required field is blank or `agent`/a reviewer is not one this agent may assign, `NotFound` for an unknown epic or blocker, and `LimitExceeded` at the board's issue cap.

signatures.signature: create_issue(title: &str, in_scope: &str, out_of_scope: &str, completion_criteria: &str, agent: &str, options: board::IssueOptions<'_>) -> Result<board::IssueCreated, ToolError>

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: in_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue covers, precisely. Part of the brief a child agent is given.

parameters.name: out_of_scope
parameters.doc: What the issue deliberately does not cover, so the work stops where it was meant to.

parameters.name: completion_criteria
parameters.doc: What must be true for the issue to be done. It is what a reviewer checks the work against.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent the issue is dispatched to. It must be one this agent may spawn.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The parts that may be left out: a description, blockers, an epic, reviewers.

functions.name: update_issue
functions.brief: Revise an issue; at least one field must be supplied.
functions.detail:
A field left at its default is left alone, `description: TextEdit::Clear` empties the description, and `epic: EpicAssignment::Ungroup` detaches the issue from its epic.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when no field was supplied or one was blanked, and `NotFound` for an unknown issue or epic id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to revise.

parameters.name: patch
parameters.doc: The fields to change. At least one; a field left at its default is left alone.

functions.name: set_issue_blocked_by
functions.brief: Replace an issue's whole blocker set; an empty slice clears every blocker.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank id or blocker, `NotFound` for an issue or blocker the board does not hold, and `Conflict` when an edge would close a cycle or block the issue on itself.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must now be done before it. An empty slice clears them all.

functions.name: remove_epic
functions.brief: Remove an epic, keeping its issues and ungrouping them.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The epic to remove.

functions.name: remove_issue
functions.brief: Remove an issue and every blocker edge pointing at it.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to remove.

functions.name: wait_for_issue
functions.brief: Register a wait on an issue and hand back an acknowledgement.
functions.detail:
Nothing blocks inside the program: the wait is recorded and the call returns at once, so the rest of the program still runs. The suspension happens after the program ends, between turns — the run frees this agent's slot until the issue is terminal, done or failed, then resumes on the next turn. It is how a turn's work is sequenced behind an issue it depends on. The issue this agent was assigned to implement is the one issue it may not wait on.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank id, or for this agent's own assigned issue, `NotFound` for an id the board does not hold, and `Unavailable` when the run has no board.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to wait on. It may not be the issue this agent was assigned.

functions.name: add_task
functions.brief: Add a task to the task graph and hand back the task budget.
functions.detail:
`options.blocked_by` names the tasks that must finish before this one, and defaults to none.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank id or title, `Conflict` on a duplicate id or an edge that would close a cycle, `NotFound` for an unknown blocker, and `LimitExceeded` at the task cap.

signatures.signature: add_task(id: &str, title: &str, options: tasks::TaskOptions<'_>) -> Result<tasks::TaskUsage, ToolError>

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The id chosen for it. Every other task call takes it, and no two tasks may share one.

parameters.name: title
parameters.doc: A short line naming the work.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The parts that may be left out: a description, and the tasks this one waits on.

functions.name: update_task
functions.brief: Revise a task's title, description or status; at least one must be supplied.
functions.detail:
A field left at its default is left alone, `description: TextEdit::Clear` empties it, and `description: TextEdit::Set(…)` replaces it.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when no field was supplied or one was blanked, and `NotFound` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to revise.

parameters.name: patch
parameters.doc: The fields to change. At least one; a field left at its default is left alone.

functions.name: set_blocked_by
functions.brief: Replace a task's whole blocker set; an empty slice clears every blocker.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank id or blocker, `NotFound` for a task or blocker that is not on the list, and `Conflict` when an edge would close a cycle or block the task on itself.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blocked_by
parameters.doc: The ids of every task that must now be done before it. An empty slice clears them all.

functions.name: complete_task
functions.brief: Mark a task done.
functions.detail:
Tasks it was blocking become actionable once every one of their blockers is done.

# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to mark done.

functions.name: remove_task
functions.brief: Remove a task and every blocker edge pointing at it.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to remove.

functions.name: write_memory
functions.brief: Record a durable memory that survives a context compaction.
functions.detail:
A memory may also carry **code**. `options.code` is a Rust module whose items are bound at `lib::<name>` in every later program this session writes, so a helper got right once is never written again; `options.on_use` is a program gg runs the first time the memory comes into use, whose views arrive on the next turn. Neither is context: they cost no window, are never shown back, and count against no body limit.

# Errors

`Conflict` on a duplicate name, and `LimitExceeded` when the body would breach the run's caps — revising or deleting a memory is the way out, rather than accruing more.

signatures.signature: write_memory(name: &str, description: &str, body: &str, options: memories::MemoryOptions<'_>) -> Result<memories::MemoryUsage, ToolError>

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. Every other memory call takes it, and no two memories may share one.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Where the run keeps a memory index this is the memory's line in it, and so all that is visible until it is read.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The memory's contents.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The code halves, which may be left out.

functions.name: update_memory
functions.brief: Replace an existing memory's description and body, keyed on its slug.
functions.detail:
Its code and on-use program are replaced too — leaving them out of `options` clears them.

# Errors

`NotFound` when no memory has that name.

signatures.signature: update_memory(name: &str, description: &str, body: &str, options: memories::MemoryOptions<'_>) -> Result<memories::MemoryUsage, ToolError>

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to replace.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: The one-line description to replace the old one with.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The contents to replace the old ones with.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The code halves. Leaving one out clears the one the memory had.

functions.name: create_memory
functions.brief: Record a new memory whose contents stay out of the context window until they are read.
functions.detail:
It takes a slug, a one-line description — required where the run keeps an index, since that is the memory's line in it — and the initial contents.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank field or a slug with characters a name may not hold, `Conflict` on a duplicate slug, and `LimitExceeded` when the contents, or the index entry, would breach a limit.

signatures.signature: create_memory(name: &str, description: &str, body: &str, options: memories::MemoryOptions<'_>) -> Result<memories::MemoryUsage, ToolError>

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`.

parameters.name: description
parameters.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds, which is its line in the index.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: The memory's initial contents, which stay out of the context window until they are read.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The code halves, which may be left out. They load on that first read.

functions.name: read_memory
functions.brief: Read one memory's full contents by slug, which is the only thing that brings them into context.
functions.detail:
A memory that carries code loads that code on being read: the reply names the `lib::<key>` it is bound at, and it stays bound for the rest of the session.

# Errors

`NotFound` when no memory has that slug.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: edit_memory
functions.brief: Revise a memory in place, replacing the one exact occurrence of `search` with `replace`.
functions.detail:
Appending is done by quoting the last line and replacing it with itself plus what is being added.

# Errors

`NotFound` when the text does not appear, `Conflict` when it appears more than once, `LimitExceeded` when the result would be too long, and `InvalidArgument` when the edit would leave the memory empty — deleting it is the way to do that.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The slug of the memory to revise.

parameters.name: search
parameters.doc: The exact text to find in its contents. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: replace
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place.

functions.name: search_memories
functions.brief: Find the memories mentioning any of `keywords`, best first.
functions.detail:
Plain case-insensitive substring matching over each memory's slug, description and contents, ranked by how many distinct keywords a memory mentions and then by how often. Several specific words rank better than one sentence; `read_memory` is what fetches a hit worth having in full. A search that matches nothing is an empty `Vec`.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when every keyword is empty.

parameters.name: keywords
parameters.doc: The words to look for. Several specific words rank better than one sentence, because a memory is ranked by how many of them it mentions.

functions.name: delete_memory
functions.brief: Evict a memory by name, freeing room in the budget.
functions.detail:
# Errors

`NotFound` when no memory has that name.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

functions.name: open_file
functions.brief: Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and closable by it.
functions.detail:
What comes back is exactly what `files::read_file` returns; the difference is the view. That split is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `options.offset` and `options.limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

# Errors

`NotFound` for a missing path, and `InvalidArgument` for an offset past the end of the file. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to show; `files::ReadOptions::default()` shows the whole file.

functions.name: open_text
functions.brief: Place a value the program computed into the context window, under `label`.
functions.detail:
A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table the program assembled. This is how the result of a program reaches the model that wrote it, and the only way it does. Opening the same label again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine a view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for an empty label — a view with no selector could never be closed or attributed — and `LimitExceeded`, naming the cap, for a body or label over gg's caps. Nothing is ever silently truncated.

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. `close` takes it, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: What to show. An empty body is allowed: it is how a program says that something it was showing is now empty.

functions.name: open_docs_view
functions.brief: Place one function's full documentation into the context window.
functions.detail:
Its signature, its description, and the declarations of any types it refers to that have not already been shown this session. This is how a function is read. It is a **view**, not a return value — the documentation arrives in the next prompt under a `Documentation` heading keyed by the function name, exactly as a file or a computed value arrives — so it is not available in the turn it is asked for. Ask in one turn, use it in the next. Opening the same function's documentation again replaces the view rather than adding a second copy, and `close` closes it.

# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown or unbound name.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The function to document, by the name it is called by in its module — `"read_file"` for `files::read_file`. Searching the documentation is what says which names exist.

functions.name: close
functions.brief: Close every view carrying `selector`, freeing the tokens they occupied.
functions.detail: For a file that is every page of that path, for a text view the one with that label, for a documentation view the function's name. Closing a selector that is not open hands back `0` rather than failing, so a program that tidies up unconditionally need not guard every call. Closing a file view forgets what was read, not what exists; closing a text view discards the only copy of what it held, so anything needed later belongs in a file or a memory first.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.doc: What the view is filed under: a file's path, a text view's label, or a documentation view's function name.

functions.name: current
functions.brief: List what is open in the context window right now.
functions.detail: Each view's `kind`, the `selector` that closes it, roughly what it costs in `tokens`, and — for a paged file view — the `region` it covers. Reading it is what decides what to close when the window is filling up.

functions.name: evict_file_view
functions.brief: Drop the contents of files that were read out of the context window, freeing the tokens they occupy.
functions.detail: The files on disk are untouched: this forgets what was read, not what exists.

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file whose views to drop; `None` drops every file view held.

functions.name: archive_thread
functions.brief: Move whole turns out of the context window and report what that reclaimed.
functions.detail:
Every result carries a header with its turn number and roughly what holding it costs, which is what names the turns worth dropping. A span is a Rust inclusive range and both ends are included, so `context::archive_thread(&[4..=19])` archives turns 4 through 19. The agent's own messages in an archived turn are dropped; the results are kept and stay searchable with `search_archive`.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for an empty list, too many spans at once, or a span that ends before it starts.

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.doc: The inclusive spans of turn numbers to move out of the window. They may overlap.

functions.name: search_archive
functions.brief: Search archived history for a case-insensitive substring, most recent first, up to 8 hits.
functions.detail: `archive_empty` is worth checking before `hits`: it distinguishes "nothing has been archived yet" from "the search ran and matched nothing", so a program does not archive again believing the first archive failed.

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The substring to look for. Matching is case-insensitive.

functions.name: compact
functions.brief: Compact the context window: the detailed thread is dropped and restarted from `summary`.
functions.detail:
A fresh read of each path in `files` is added to the restarted window. Skills, memories and the task list are kept as they are. gg asks for this call when the window is full, and refuses every other call until it arrives.

It does not stop the program: it registers the request and returns, and the rewrite happens once the program has ended. Everything not in the summary and not in `files` is gone, so the summary is written for the agent that comes after and `files` names what it will need in hand.

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What the restarted window opens with. Everything not in it and not re-read from `files` is gone.

parameters.name: files
parameters.doc: The paths to read afresh into the restarted window. An empty slice reads nothing back.

functions.name: spawn_subagent
functions.brief: Delegate scoped work to a child agent and hand back its handle immediately.
functions.detail:
The child runs in parallel while the program continues. `agent` names one of the agent profiles this agent may spawn — the system prompt lists them, and the profile selects the child's model, tools and instructions. The brief is either `Brief::Prompt("self-contained instructions")` or `Brief::Issue("AUTH-1")`. The child shares the workspace.

# Errors

`LimitExceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `InvalidArgument` when `agent` is not one this agent may spawn.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent profile to run the child as, from the ones this agent may spawn. It selects the child's model, tools and instructions.

parameters.name: brief
parameters.doc: What the child is to do: `Brief::Prompt` with self-contained instructions, or `Brief::Issue` with the id of a board issue to brief it from.

functions.name: wait_for_subagents
functions.brief: Block until the named children have finished and collect their results in dispatch order.
functions.detail:
With `None` it waits for every outstanding child. The run's wall-clock budget keeps running throughout, so one wait for many children costs far less than one wait per child.

# Errors

`NotFound` for an id this agent did not spawn.

parameters.name: ids
parameters.doc: The children to wait for, as `spawn_subagent` returned them; `None` waits for every one still outstanding.

functions.name: send_message
functions.brief: Deliver a message to a running child agent's inbox, which it reads at its next turn.
functions.detail:
`SubagentHandle::send` is the same call with the id already supplied, for the common case where the handle is in hand.

# Errors

`NotFound` for an unknown agent id, and `Conflict` when that child has already returned.

parameters.name: agent_id
parameters.doc: The child to deliver to, as `spawn_subagent` returned it.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. It reads it at its next turn.

functions.name: transition_state
functions.brief: Move the process this session is running inside on to another of its states.
functions.detail:
The state is named the way an agent to spawn is named. It is bound only when a state machine is driving the session and the current state has somewhere to go. Like `context::compact` it is registered rather than performed: the call validates the target, returns, and the program runs on to its end, because replacing the agent — and its window — mid-program would pull every remaining call out from under it. The first declaration in a turn is the one that stands.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a state this session may not move to, `Refused` for a second declaration in one turn, and `Unavailable` when this agent is not running inside a state machine at all.

parameters.name: state
parameters.doc: The state to move on to, named the way an agent to spawn is named.

parameters.name: note
parameters.doc: The opening message the next state's agent sees; `None` tells it nothing.

functions.name: exec
functions.brief: Continue this session as a different agent, from the next turn.
functions.detail:
The named agent takes over with its own model, tools and instructions, keeping every capability the two of them share — the whole conversation above all, so it needs no catching up. Registered rather than performed, exactly as `transition_state` is and for the same reason: the window would otherwise be pulled out from under the program still composing into it. A session makes one succession per turn. It is bound only when this agent may make agent transitions and has agents it may become, and never while a state machine is driving the session.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for an agent this session may not become, `Refused` for a second succession in one turn, and `Unavailable` when this agent is running inside a machine, which is left by `transition_state` instead.

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent to become, from the ones this agent may become.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Its opening message. It already has the whole conversation, so this is the instruction rather than a briefing; `None` tells it nothing.

functions.name: fork
functions.brief: Run a copy of this agent, in parallel, on something it will not do itself.
functions.detail:
The copy has the same model, the same tools and a private copy of the whole conversation, so `prompt` is the *difference* rather than a briefing — everything already worked out is already there.

Its handle comes back immediately, but the copy itself starts once this turn's tool results are recorded, because the conversation it inherits has to be a complete one. So `wait_for_subagents` can only collect it on a later turn, and waiting on it in the program that made it never returns it.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank prompt, `LimitExceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `Unavailable` when the run has no delegation runtime to copy this agent into.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: What the copy is to do instead. It has the whole conversation already, so this is the difference rather than a briefing.

functions.name: read_skill
functions.brief: Read a skill by name and hand back its body with the front matter stripped.
functions.detail:
Reading it also pins that body permanently into context, so a skill that has been read stays read.

A skill may be **code** rather than prose, or as well as it. Code is bound at `lib::<key>` for the rest of the session and the reply names the key and what it offers. An on-use program runs once this program has ended, and whatever it shows arrives on the next turn.

# Errors

`NotFound` — listing the skills that do exist — when the name is unknown.

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The skill's name, as the system prompt lists it.

functions.name: history
functions.brief: List the programs this session has already run, oldest first.
functions.detail:
Each carries the turn it ran on, how big it was, and whether it ran to its end. It lists shapes, not sources: `get` is what fetches one. The list survives a compaction, so it is also how a program whose text has left the context window is found again. A session that has run nothing yet gets an empty `Vec` rather than an error.

# Errors

`Unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library — which is a different fact from an empty one, and the reason this hands back a `Result` rather than a bare `Vec`.

functions.name: get
functions.brief: Fetch the exact source of one program that ran, as a `String`; `None` fetches the most recent.
functions.detail:
This is the first half of fixing a program without rewriting it: get what ran, patch it with ordinary string work, and hand the result to `rerun`. What comes back is the program that **executed**, so when a turn's program was itself handed over by `rerun`, the program that ran is what arrives rather than the few lines that asked for it — and fetch-patch-run composes turn after turn.

# Errors

`NotFound`, naming the turns that are held, for a turn that ran no program or one old enough that the library has dropped it, and `Unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library.

parameters.name: turn
parameters.doc: The turn whose program to fetch, as `history` reports it; `None` fetches the most recent one.

functions.name: rerun
functions.brief: Hand gg a program to run in place of this one.
functions.detail:
The calling program finishes, then gg compiles and runs `source` as this turn's program. Used with `get` it fixes a program without re-emitting it. Nothing is undone: every call the calling program already made stands, and the program that runs next sees the world it left behind — so the hand-over belongs before work that should not happen twice.

The first call stands, because a silently replaced program is a change nobody can see. If the calling program then fails, the hand-over is cancelled along with everything else that program decided, and the turn ends in an ordinary error. Chains are bounded: one hand-over per turn, and the fixed program is the one that does the work.

# Errors

`Refused` for a second hand-over in one turn, `InvalidArgument` for a blank source, and `Unavailable` when this agent keeps no program library.

parameters.name: source
parameters.doc: The program to run in place of this one, as Rust. It may not be blank.

functions.name: finish
functions.brief: End the session, reporting what was done in a sentence or two.
functions.detail:
This is the only thing that ends a working agent's session. It does not stop the program — whatever follows it still runs — so it belongs last, once the tools have confirmed the work is really done. A program that then fails has the ending cancelled and gets another turn.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` for a blank summary, and `Unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What was done, in a sentence or two.

functions.name: approve
functions.brief: Accept the work under review: it meets every completion criterion and stays in scope.
functions.detail:
This ends the session. It does not stop the program — whatever follows it still runs — so it belongs last, once the change has actually been read. It takes nothing, because an approval carries no obligation beyond itself.

# Errors

`Unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

functions.name: request_changes
functions.brief: Reject the work under review, listing every change that must be made before it can be accepted.
functions.detail:
This ends the session, and does not stop the program. Each item says what is wrong and what to change.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when the list is empty, and `Unavailable` when this agent's role ends its session some other way.

parameters.name: items
parameters.doc: Every change that must be made before the work can be accepted, one per entry: what is wrong, and what to change. It may not be empty.

functions.name: send
functions.brief: Deliver a message to this child's inbox, which it reads at its next turn.
functions.detail:
`send_message` with the id already supplied, for the common case where the handle is in hand.

# Errors

`Conflict` when this child has already returned.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox.

types.name: TextEdit
types.declaration: enum TextEdit<'a> { Keep, Clear, Set(&'a str) }
types.brief: A three-way edit of an optional text field: leave it, empty it, or replace it.
types.detail:
It is an `enum` because the field really has three states: an `Option<&str>` could say only two, and would make "clear it" and "set it to the empty string" one request.

`Keep` is the `Default`, so a patch built with `..Default::default()` leaves the field alone — which is what leaving a field out of a patch has to mean. The board's `IssuePatch` takes the same type.
